title: Participles and the infinitive

objectives.can: Recognise the Peal active and passive participles and the infinitive, and parse the participles' gender, number and state.

explanation.summary: A participle is a verbal adjective: it describes someone as doing (active) or as having had something done to them (passive), and it agrees with a noun in gender, number and state. In Biblical Aramaic it is also one of the commonest forms of a clause's main verb. The infinitive names the action itself and is nearly always found after a prefixed ל-.

sections.heading: The active participle
body: The Peal active participle has a long vowel after the first consonant and a short one, or a long one, after the second: אָמַר 'saying', יָדַע 'knowing', עָבֵד 'doing, making'. Participles of verbs with a weak last consonant end in a vowel letter: עָנֵה 'answering', חָזֵה 'seeing'.

A participle is inflected like an adjective, so it shows gender, number and state. The masculine singular absolute is the plain form, as in the examples above. The masculine plural absolute ends in -ִין: אָמְרִין 'saying', יָדְעִין 'knowing', פָּלְחִין 'serving'. The feminine singular absolute ends in -ָה: כָתְבָה 'writing'. The feminine plural absolute ends in -ָן: סָלְקָן 'coming up'. These endings are the same as the endings of nouns (A1.1.1).

sections.heading: State: absolute, construct and determined
body: Like a noun, a participle can stand in the absolute state (as a predicate, or an adjective with an indefinite noun), the construct (a participle that governs a following noun: דָּיְרֵי 'dwellers of') or the determined (a participle used with a determined noun, like יָקִדְתָּא 'burning' in the phrase for the burning fiery furnace). The state ending is added to the participle as it is added to nouns. The masculine plural construct ends in -ֵי: דָּיְרֵי, יָדְעֵי 'knowers of'.

Most participles in the texts are in the absolute state: about 185 of the Peal participles are absolute, ten are construct and eleven are determined. Learn to parse them for gender, number and state in that order.

sections.heading: The passive participle
body: The passive participle looks back at what has been done to its subject: 'blessed', 'known', 'written'. In the Peal its pattern has a long ִי after the second consonant: בְּרִיךְ 'blessed', גְּמִיר 'finished, completed', דְּחִיל 'feared, fearsome', חֲשִׁיבִין 'reckoned', יְדִיעַ 'known'. It is declined for gender, number and state in the same way.

The texts label most of these participles with the stem name Peil, and a few with Peal; both labels describe the same pattern. This course treats the passive participle together with the active participle because they are the two participles of the simple stem. The Peil perfect, in which the same inner vowels appear, is taught in A3.1.

sections.heading: The infinitive
body: The Peal infinitive begins with מ-, and nearly always follows the preposition ל-: לְמִבְנֵא 'to build', לְמֵאמַר 'to say', לְמֶעְבַּד 'to do', לְמִקְרֵא 'to read', לְמִנְתַּן 'to give'. A few verbs have an infinitive without the מ-, as in לִבְּנֵא (also 'to build', Ezra 5:3). The ל- may be replaced by another preposition, as in וּכְמִצְבְּיֵהּ 'and according to his wanting', where the infinitive has a pronoun suffix.

The infinitive can have a subject or an object like a verb. It is used for purpose ('to build the house'), for the content of a command or a wish, and after verbs of ability and beginning. The forms are few in the texts. The infinitive of the Pael, the Haphel and the other stems is taught in A2.2.

sections.heading: Why the participle matters
body: In Biblical Aramaic the participle is much more than an adjective. It is common as the main verb of a clause, for the present ('they are serving') and for events in a story: עָנֵה וְאָמַר, 'he answered and said', is the usual way of introducing a speech in Daniel, in a participle for each verb. In the plural it is עָנַיִן וְאָמְרִין. The syntax of the participle is the subject of A4.1.3; here the task is only to recognise the forms and parse them.

misunderstandings: A participle is not tied to past time. עָנֵה וְאָמַר may be about a past event, and a participle in another sentence may be about the present. Read the whole clause.
The active participle אָמַר (with long a after the first consonant) is not the same word as the perfect אֲמַר (with a reduced vowel). Look at the vowel after the first consonant.
A participle has no person. Do not look for 'he' or 'I' in its form: the subject is a noun or a pronoun in the sentence, and when none is given the context supplies it.
A participle in -ִין looks like a noun in -ִין, since both are masculine plural absolute. Check whether the word is a verb in its verse before you parse it.

deeper.heading: Active and passive participles in different labels
body: The analysed texts use the label Peil for the passive of the simple stem, in the participle and in the perfect, and they label a few passive participles Peal. This is a matter of the dataset's labelling and not a difference in the language. When a form has the pattern with the long ִי, treat it as the passive participle of the simple stem.

quoted.english: The king answered and said to the Chaldeans: 'The thing is certain with me; if ye make not known unto me the dream and the interpretation thereof, ye shall be cut in pieces, and your houses shall be made a dunghill.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: עָנֵה and וְאָמַר are Peal participles, masculine singular absolute. Together they mean 'he answered and said', and the first participle shows that this is the usual way of introducing a speech. The subject is 'the king'; the participle itself has no person. Notice that the vowel after the first consonant of וְאָמַר is long, which marks the participle against the perfect אֲמַר.

examples.analysis: סָלְקָן and שָׁנְיָן are feminine plural participles in the absolute state, with the ending -ָן. They agree with חֵיוָן, 'beasts', which is feminine plural; the first means 'coming up', the second 'differing'. Here the participle is a description of a scene as it is seen, a use that is taught in A4.1.3.

examples.analysis: לְמִבְנֵא is the Peal infinitive of the verb 'build', after ל-: 'to build'. The leaders of the people rose up and began to build. The verb וְשָׁרִיו before it (position 8) is a Pael, and the infinitive tells what they began to do.
